test.title: Three ways to cross a river

paragraphs.text: Engineers choose the type of bridge largely according to the distance it must cross. For short distances, a beam bridge is usually the simplest solution: a flat deck rests on supports at each end. Beam bridges are cheap to build, but without extra supports in the middle they rarely span more than about 80 metres.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Arch bridges carry their load outwards along a curve to the ground at each end. They have been built for thousands of years, originally from stone and today usually from concrete or steel. Because the arch pushes against the ground, it needs firm rock at both ends, and the longest steel arches span around 550 metres.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: For the widest crossings, engineers use suspension bridges. Here the deck hangs from vertical cables attached to two main cables, which pass over tall towers and are anchored in huge blocks of concrete on land. Suspension bridges can span more than 1,900 metres, but they can move in strong winds, so modern decks are shaped to let the air flow smoothly around them.
paragraphs.label: C
